ch2_p7_periodicity_sim_solo.text: Welcome to the Spectral Periodicity and Resonance Workbench. Adjust cycle period P, sampling stride k, amplitude A, and start seed r. Observe how stride k equal to period P locks into identical wave phases, creating severe estimation bias. Drag stride k to a coprime value like 8 or 11 to break resonance and restore unbiased sampling.

ch2_p7_periodicity_sim_duo.text: Check out the live wave canvas! When stride k matches cycle period P, every sample lands right on the same wave crest, triggering the red Resonance Alert. Drag stride k to 8 to see the points distribute evenly across all wave phases, dropping harmonic bias to zero!

ch2_p7_chk1_solo.text: Active Checkpoint 1. In Vitter's Reservoir Sampling Algorithm R with buffer size k equals 100, item 1,001 arrives. What is the exact conditional probability that an item already inside the reservoir at step 1,000 remains intact? Select your answer.

ch2_p7_chk1_duo.text: Active Checkpoint 1! An existing reservoir item only gets ejected if the new item enters and picks that specific item's slot. Calculate the survival probability and choose Option A, B, C, or D!

ch2_p7_chk1_feedback_correct.text: Outstanding! Option B is correct. An existing item survives if the new item either is not chosen, or replaces a different slot. The probability is 1 minus 1 over n plus 1, which equals n over n plus 1. For n equal to 1,000, that is exactly 1,000 over 1,001!

ch2_p7_chk1_feedback_incorrect.text: Incorrect. Remember the inductive step: the new item enters with probability k over n plus 1, and chooses a specific slot with probability 1 over k. The replacement probability is therefore 1 over n plus 1, meaning the survival probability is 1 minus 1 over n plus 1, or n over n plus 1. The correct answer is Option B.

ch2_p7_rds_sim_solo.text: Welcome to the Respondent-Driven Sampling Degree Bias Workbench. Use the sliders to adjust hub degree, normal degree, and hub population fraction. Notice how high-degree hubs dominate the naive snowball draw, inflating the sample mean. Then observe how the Volz-Heckathorn inverse-degree weighting completely eliminates this distortion, snapping the estimate back to true population mean.

ch2_p7_rds_sim_duo.text: Look at the bar comparison! High-degree hubs are only 10 percent of the true population, but they make up over 50 percent of the naive snowball sample, doubling the apparent mean! But look at the Volz-Heckathorn RDS bar: inverse degree weighting snaps the estimate right back to ground truth!

ch2_p7_chk2_solo.text: Active Checkpoint 2. In an RDS study, Participant A reports 40 contacts, while Participant B reports 4 contacts. Under the Volz-Heckathorn estimator, what is the relative ratio of their sampling weights w-sub-B over w-sub-A? Select Option A, B, C, or D.

ch2_p7_chk2_duo.text: Active Checkpoint 2! Participant A has 40 contacts, and Participant B has 4 contacts. Under Volz-Heckathorn inverse-degree weighting, which participant gets weighted higher and by how much? Make your choice!

ch2_p7_chk2_feedback_correct.text: Spot on! Option C is correct. Under Respondent-Driven Sampling, selection probability is proportional to network degree d-sub-i. Therefore, sampling weights are inversely proportional: w-sub-i equals 1 over d-sub-i. Participant B, with 4 contacts, receives 1 fourth, while Participant A receives 1 fortieth. Dividing 1 fourth by 1 fortieth yields a 10x higher weight for Participant B!

ch2_p7_chk2_feedback_incorrect.text: Not quite. Remember that in Respondent-Driven Sampling, highly connected hubs are structurally oversampled by peer referrals. To neutralize this bias, we must apply inverse degree weighting: w-sub-i equals 1 over d-sub-i. 1 over 4 divided by 1 over 40 equals 10. Participant B receives 10 times the weight of Participant A. The correct answer is Option C.
